Description: Report to the President and Congress on federally funded research and development in networking and information technology., The United States leads the world in networking and information technology (NIT), impacting scientific discovery, human health, education, the environment, national security, transportation, manufacturing, energy, and governance. The Federal Government coordinates NIT research and development through the NITRD program. PCAST reviews progress and makes recommendations for continued investment in NIT R&D., The document reviews the NITRD program, assessing progress on recommendations made in 2010 and making further recommendations in response to activities and advances since 2010., Notable progress in multi-agency investments in big data, health IT, cybersecurity, social computing, privacy, software technology, educational technology, energy and transportation, network scaling, and high-performance computing. Emphasis on cross-agency collaboration and coordination., Discussion on the structure and coordination of NITRD, the role of SSGs, the importance of NIT education, and recommendations for strategic investments in NIT R&D., Recommendations for initiatives and investments in NIT R&D to achieve America's priorities and advance key NIT research frontiers, including big data, health IT, cybersecurity, social computing, privacy R&D, educational technologies, dynamic power management, and high-performance computing., This report assesses the status and direction of the Federal Networking and Information Technology Research and Development (NITRD) Program, providing an update to the 2010 review and assessing responses to the 2010 recommendations., The report reviews the impact of Networking and Information Technology (NIT) on various aspects of life, including economic growth, scientific discovery, and national priorities. It discusses the progress made since the 2010 recommendations and highlights the importance of effective coordination of NIT R&D investments., Federally-funded research in both universities and industry leads to technological innovations creating new product categories and industries. Advances in technical areas like big data and social computing have enabled growth in sectors such as cloud computing and social networking. Grand challenges in NIT R&D align with national priorities, focusing on robotics, secure internet, personalized education, health monitoring, and data-driven science., The review focuses on the progress in responding to the recommendations made in the 2010 PCAST NITRD report, which included initiatives in NIT for health, energy, transportation, and cyber-infrastructure security, as well as investment in fundamental NIT research frontiers and core technologies., The document discusses the increasing volumes of data generated from various sources and the initiatives taken by federal agencies to manage and analyze this data. It highlights the 'Big Data Initiative' launched by the OSTP in 2012 with significant R&D investments and the National Robotics Initiative to enhance American manufacturing., Research in embedded systems and cyber-physical systems, progress in health IT and interagency collaboration, federal agencies' support for R&D in robotics and health IT, coordination of research initiatives, potential of NIT in health and healthcare, data mining and machine learning in health information, development of interoperable health records and systems., The 2010 NITRD report identified cybersecurity as an area of great and growing importance, emphasizing the need for new approaches and significant investment in long-term research. The report highlights the coordination efforts of various federal groups and the importance of improving cybersecurity infrastructure., The 2010 NITRD report recommended collaborative research in social computing and privacy protection. NSF, DARPA, and HHS have independent programs in social computing. A coordinated cross-agency initiative is recommended. Privacy challenges require a practical science of privacy protection., The document discusses the challenges and recommendations for privacy R&D, software technology, and educational technology within the NITRD program. It emphasizes the need for interagency collaboration and sustained research efforts., The document discusses the assessment of technology use in education and energy, highlighting the need for coordinated R&D efforts and the role of various government agencies., The report discusses the creation of a nationwide infrastructure for spectrum monitoring, the Spectrum Sharing Innovation Test-Bed Pilot Program, and the Enhancing Access to Radio Spectrum (EARS) solicitation. It highlights the importance of system and network scaling, and the need for continued investment in high-performance computing (HPC) research and development., The document discusses the need for a coordinated program for research on architectures, algorithms, and software for next-generation HPC systems, and the importance of balancing investments in NIT R&D and infrastructure. It also reviews progress in recommendations for improving NITRD coordination., Discussion on the structure and evolution of NITRD coordination, the role of SSGs, agency participation, and budget transparency recommendations., Challenges in transparent reporting of NITRD funding, recommendations for improving budget reporting and assessment of government investments in NIT R&D., The document discusses the importance of NIT education for innovators, workers, and citizens, highlighting the need for education from childhood through adulthood. It emphasizes the role of federal investment in NIT research and development and the need for strategic investments to address national priorities., The report discusses the need for a national strategy for R&D investment in NIT, recommending the establishment of a high-level standing committee to provide strategic advice. It highlights the importance of NIT for health, energy, and transportation., Recommendations for federal investment in NIT research across various sectors including power management, national security, education, digital democracy, privacy, human-computer interaction, and data management., Recommendations for continued investment in NIT R&D core areas, scalable systems and networking, software creation and evolution, high-performance computing, and education and human resources., Recommendations for improving NITRD budget reporting categories and federal leadership in NIT R&D investments., Acknowledgments of contributors and list of acronyms related to various organizations and initiatives.

Description: Second assessment and recommendations of the National Nanotechnology Advisory Panel, established to review the Federal nanotechnology research and development program., The report assesses the National Nanotechnology Initiative, providing recommendations to strengthen the program, including expanding communication efforts, developing standards for nanomaterial identification, and coordinating environmental, health, and safety research., The report is the second NNAP review of the National Nanotechnology Initiative (NNI), updating the first assessment published in 2005. It discusses the NNI budget request for fiscal year 2009, the total NNI investment since 2001, and the global investment in nanotechnology., The report discusses the progress and challenges in nanotechnology, focusing on technology transfer, environmental, health, and safety research, education, and societal dimensions. It highlights the United States' leadership in nanotechnology, the importance of infrastructure investment, and the need for continued EHS research and ethical considerations., The NNAP provides recommendations for strengthening the NNI, focusing on infrastructure, management, coordination, standards development, and technology transfer., The document discusses the progress and recommendations for the National Nanotechnology Initiative (NNI), focusing on innovation, commercialization, environmental, health, safety, societal, ethical implications, and communication outreach. It highlights the importance of integrating societal and ethical research with technical R&D and emphasizes the need for effective communication to avoid public misconceptions., The National Nanotechnology Initiative (NNI) coordinates nanotechnology activities across the Federal Government, involving 25 Federal agencies with a collective R&D budget of $1.5 billion in FY 2009. The NNI is overseen by the National Science and Technology Council and the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, with regular assessments by the National Academies and Government Accountability Office., The document discusses the United States' leadership in nanotechnology research and development, the role of federal investment, and recommendations for strengthening the NNI, including technology transfer, environmental and health implications, societal implications, and education/workforce preparation., The report represents the second biennial review of the National Nanotechnology Initiative by PCAST in its capacity as the NNAP. It includes assessments and recommendations on nanotechnology research, development, education, technology transfer, commercialization, environmental, health, and safety issues, as well as societal and ethical concerns., U.S. investment in nanotechnology research and development continues to grow, with Federal funding increasing from $982 million in FY 2005 to $1.53 billion in FY 2009. The growth rate has slowed, but international private sector funding has also increased, with total public and private sector support for nanotechnology R&D reaching $13.9 billion worldwide as of 2007., The document discusses the challenges and metrics for measuring progress in nanotechnology research, development, and commercialization, highlighting the role of the NNI in supporting research infrastructure and the United States' leadership in publications and citations., Analysis of nanotechnology publications and patents, including trends in patent filings and international collaboration efforts., The United States is involved in the OECD working parties on nanotechnology and manufactured nanomaterials, leading efforts in environmental, health, and safety. The NNI Strategic Plan update retains strategic investment areas and divides the Societal Dimensions PCA into Environment, Health and Safety, and Education and Societal Dimensions. The NNAP recommends legislative changes for NNI oversight. The NNI plays a central role in nanotechnology innovation and commercialization., Challenges and economic impact of nanotechnology development, manufacturing, and marketing, including venture capital investment in new nanotechnology-based firms by state from 1995-2006., The document discusses the development and commercialization of nanotechnology, focusing on consumer products, biomedicine, energy, and electronics. It highlights the use of nanoscale metal oxides in sunscreens and the ongoing research on their safety., The document discusses the development of a diagnostic nanotechnology known as the biobarcode assay by researchers at Northwestern University, which can simultaneously detect trace levels of multiple biomarkers associated with human cancers. It also covers the use of dendrimers as targeted delivery vehicles for anticancer therapy by researchers at the University of Michigan., The use of G5 dendrimers in cancer treatment, the development of thin-film photovoltaic technology by Nanosolar, Inc., and the potential of titanium-studded carbon nanotubes for hydrogen storage., Research on carbon nanotubes for hydrogen storage and IBM's development of molecular switches and magnetic anisotropy measurement for data storage., The document discusses the challenges and barriers to commercialization of nanotechnology, the role of the Federal Government and NNI in overcoming these barriers, and the implications of addressing environmental, health, safety, and ethics issues responsibly., The document discusses the role of Federal agencies in supporting EHS research related to nanotechnology, the importance of strategic funding, and the need for collaboration with industry and international research agencies. It highlights the concerns about public acceptance of nanotechnology and the importance of responsible development., Input from public comment and Federal nanotechnology EHS research analyses informed the development of the NNI's 2008 strategy for nanotechnology-related EHS research. Federal agencies have been proactive in addressing EHS information needs and regulatory approaches., The document discusses the environmental, health, and safety (EHS) implications of nanotechnology, emphasizing the need for strategic research guided by scientifically determined priorities and standardized methods. It highlights the role of the NNI and Federal Government in developing tests for environmental effects of nanoscale materials and the importance of collaboration with industry, academia, and international peers., The report discusses the importance of characterizing nanoscale materials, the application of nanotechnology in health, safety concerns in workplaces, and ethical implications., Discussion on the ethical implications of nanotechnology, coordination among agencies, and recommendations for sustaining leadership through strategy and communication., Discussion on the role of the National Nanotechnology Initiative in maintaining U.S. leadership in nanotechnology, recommendations for infrastructure, management, and coordination improvements., The document discusses the importance of multidisciplinary research in nanotechnology, the need for improved intra-agency coordination, and the development of standards for nanomaterials. It highlights the roles of various agencies in fostering nanotechnology research and development, and emphasizes the importance of standards for commercialization and safety., Nanotechnology innovation through to commercialization depends on maintaining and strengthening cross-sector collaborations and cross-fertilization of technology development and business development expertise. Efforts to assess national and international innovation and commercialization activities are needed, along with building connections across the innovation ecosystem and educating more scientists and engineers to become entrepreneurs and skilled technology workers. Environmental, Health, and Safety Implications of nanotechnology must be strategically guided, integrated, and coordinated across agencies, sectors, and countries., The document discusses the integration of implications research with applications research in nanotechnology, the development of joint programs among NNI agencies, the distribution of nonproprietary information about nanomaterials, societal and ethical implications of nanotechnology, and communication and outreach efforts to inform public perception., Program Component Areas (PCAs) are the major subject areas under which related NNI projects and activities are grouped. These areas cut across the interests and needs of the participating agencies and indicate where advancement may be expedited through coordination of work by multiple agencies., Part 30/34 of OCR content detailing various aspects of nanoscale phenomena, processes, materials, devices, systems, instrumentation, manufacturing, research facilities, environment, health, safety, education, and societal dimensions related to nanotechnology., The document summarizes key findings and recommendations from the 2006 NRC review of the National Nanotechnology Initiative (NNI), highlighting the impact of NNI-related R&D, interagency cooperation, strategic goals, and the development of multidisciplinary research centers., The document discusses the investment, innovation, and economic impact of nanotechnology, along with recommendations for federal government actions and research priorities., Reports and studies on nanotechnology, including hazard identification, patent studies, and safety guidelines., This report was prepared for publication by the National Nanotechnology Coordination Office (NNCO).

Description: A report prepared by the Steering Committee of the Advanced Manufacturing Partnership 2.0 (AMP2.0) to address the challenge of expanding advanced manufacturing across the United States., The AMP2.0 report outlines strategic steps for advancing U.S. manufacturing capabilities, including the development of a Federal strategic plan and leveraging Federal organizations to improve information flow to manufacturers., The report discusses the state of U.S. manufacturing, the challenges faced, and recommendations for innovation, talent pipeline, and business climate improvements., The report discusses the importance of U.S. manufacturing competitiveness, the role of advanced technologies, and recommendations for establishing a national strategy for securing U.S. advantage in emerging manufacturing technologies., The document discusses the importance of coordinating public and private investment in emerging manufacturing technologies, recommending the creation of an Advanced Manufacturing Advisory Consortium and manufacturing centers of excellence., The document discusses the establishment of manufacturing centers of excellence and manufacturing technology testbeds to support advanced manufacturing R&D. It emphasizes the importance of developing standards and interoperability for manufacturing new products and processes, including cybersecurity process certification., The document discusses the establishment of the National Network for Manufacturing Innovation (NNMI) to address technology challenges and secure the talent pipeline in manufacturing through public-private partnerships., The AMP2.0 SC recommends launching a national campaign to change the image of manufacturing and support National Manufacturing Day. It also focuses on connecting Americans with skills for successful careers in manufacturing through skills certifications, apprenticeships, and community college investments., The Advanced Manufacturing Partnership provided recommendations for career education pathways, online training programs, veteran transition to manufacturing careers, and the role of educational institutions in workforce development., The document discusses strategies for small and medium manufacturers to adopt manufacturing technologies through intermediary services, improve capital access, and enhance information flow. It includes recommendations for leveraging existing organizations and creating investment funds to reduce risks associated with advanced manufacturing scale-up., The report describes the Advanced Manufacturing Partnership 2.0's actions and recommendations for accelerating progress in U.S. advanced manufacturing through innovation, talent development, and business climate improvement., The report discusses the Advanced Manufacturing Partnership launched by President Obama in 2011, its recommendations, and the subsequent AMP2.0 phase. It focuses on enabling innovation, securing the talent pipeline, and improving the business climate to enhance U.S. manufacturing competitiveness., Recommendations for securing U.S. leadership in advanced manufacturing through innovation, talent development, and business climate improvement., The document discusses the implementation of recommendations for advanced manufacturing, focusing on innovation, shared infrastructure, and the establishment of a National Manufacturing Technology Strategy., The document discusses the United States' approach to developing national technology strategies for advanced manufacturing, emphasizing public-private partnerships and prioritization of key manufacturing technology areas. It highlights three transformative manufacturing technologies: Advanced Sensing, Control, and Platforms for Manufacturing (ASCPM); Visualization, Informatics and Digital Manufacturing Technologies (VIDM); and Advanced Materials Manufacturing (AMM)., The document discusses the rapid development of novel materials due to advanced modeling technology and high-throughput research. It highlights the importance of materials innovation for U.S. competitiveness and national security. AMP2.0 has prepared analyses on advanced structural composites, biomanufacturing, and critical materials reprocessing. The document outlines technology strategy recommendations for prioritized manufacturing technology areas, emphasizing public-private partnerships and the role of federal research and development agencies., Recommendations for establishing a national strategy for securing U.S. advantage in emerging manufacturing technologies, creating an Advanced Manufacturing Advisory Consortium, and establishing a new public-private manufacturing research and development infrastructure., Discussion on the need for manufacturing centers of excellence and manufacturing technology testbeds to support advanced manufacturing R&D and technology adoption., The report discusses the role of manufacturing centers of excellence and technology testbeds in supporting manufacturing technologies, the need for industry-driven standards, and the establishment of the National Network for Manufacturing Innovation., Recommendation to create a shared National Network for Manufacturing Innovation governance structure, focus on securing the talent pipeline in manufacturing, and shifting public perceptions of manufacturing., A layered approach to change the image of American manufacturing and connect Americans with skills for successful careers in manufacturing, leveraging National Manufacturing Day and public-private partnerships., The report discusses efforts to address the skills gap in manufacturing through credentialing programs and apprenticeships, highlighting best practices, challenges, and recommendations for increasing the use of nationally portable and stackable credentials., Development of apprenticeship models and career pathways in manufacturing, focusing on skills credentials, accreditations, and partnerships with educational institutions., The document discusses best-in-class curriculum for K-12 and higher education focusing on advanced manufacturing education, workforce development, and career pathways. It highlights the importance of online training, accreditation programs, and the role of veterans in bridging the skills gap., AMP2.0 developed bridging modules for transitioning U.S. Veterans to private sector manufacturing skills certifications. It created tools and guides for veterans, employers, and colleges to aid in transitioning veterans to civilian careers. Description: An advisory report by the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology on improving health care and reducing costs through systems engineering., Report by the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology on improving health care through systems engineering., The report discusses the application of systems engineering in health care, outlining goals for improvement and providing examples of successful implementations., The document discusses the expansion of access to the health-care system, the importance of affordable and high-quality care, and the role of systems-engineering approaches in improving health care. It also outlines recommendations for aligning payment incentives, developing health-data infrastructure, and training health professionals., Recommendations for improving health-care systems through systems engineering, data analytics, and community engagement., The document discusses the need to center health care on patients, families, and population health, highlighting the importance of systems engineering in improving health care quality and efficiency. It references the Affordable Care Act and the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act as policies supporting these initiatives., Systems engineering is an interdisciplinary approach to analyze, design, manage, and measure complex systems to improve efficiency, productivity, quality, safety, and other factors in health care. It includes tools and methods like industrial engineering, Lean, operations management, and more., Denver Health used the Toyota Production System to redesign operations, achieving significant successes such as reducing serious conditions and saving costs while increasing uncompensated care., Kaiser Permanente uses systems engineering and performance improvement tools to enhance care delivery, including a sepsis mortality reduction initiative. Vanderbilt University Medical Center's MyHealthTeam model improves chronic disease management and care coordination using health information technology., The project has experienced several challenges in scaling the model to larger populations and additional clinical groups. Barriers to greater use of systems methods and tools include the lack of quality and performance measures and the misaligned incentive structure of the predominant fee-for-service payment system., Discussion on the increase in hospital-owned physician practices, barriers to systems engineering in small practices, and recommendations for improving health care delivery through systems engineering., Discussion on the impact of changing payment systems in healthcare, using Virginia Mason Medical Center as a case study, and the role of the Affordable Care Act in promoting better health outcomes at lower costs., Recommendations to accelerate the transition to outcomes-based payments, promote transparency, and provide tools and supports for practice transformation. Discusses the importance of expanding clinical and operational data for improvement initiatives and the role of electronic health records and patient-generated health data., The document discusses the development of health IT infrastructure, focusing on EHR interoperability, patient-generated health data, and policy options for advancing health IT., Accelerate the creation of a robust health-data infrastructure through widespread adoption of interoperable electronic health records and advances in data exchange. Leverage HHS data for benchmarking performance and understanding health trends., Researchers can access Medicare claims data through CMS' VRDC. CMS provides ACOs with monthly claims feeds. CMS shares Medicare data with States and qualified entities for quality reporting. Medicare enrollees have access to their claims information. CMS releases provider-level Medicare data to promote transparency. CMS released hospital charges data and services data for Medicare beneficiaries. EIA serves as an independent source of energy information. Additional health data sources include Federal Employee Health Benefit Program, VHA, DoD, and PCORI., The document discusses the need for HHS to leverage existing data resources to improve health outcomes through systems engineering. It recommends creating a senior leadership position to focus on healthcare transformation, expanding access to data, and collaborating with federal and private partners. It also highlights the importance of technical support for healthcare professionals and communities in applying systems-engineering approaches., Efforts to expand technical assistance in systems engineering in health care, including initiatives by VHA, CMS, and AHRQ, and the role of RECs in supporting EHR adoption., The document discusses the application of systems-engineering principles in healthcare, emphasizing community partnerships and system-based design. It highlights examples such as Jeffrey Brenner's work in Camden and the rebuilding of New Orleans' healthcare infrastructure post-Hurricane Katrina., An initiative by Queen of the Valley Medical Center to reduce hospital readmissions and emergency-room use for low-income and vulnerable adults using the CARE Network. The program showed promising results with significant reductions in hospitalizations and emergency room visits., The document discusses the Beacon Community Program and its efforts to improve population health through health IT and care delivery redesign. It highlights the Southeast Minnesota Beacon Community's initiatives to enhance data exchange and EHR use, and the role of community health needs assessments in fostering partnerships and systems-engineering activities., Recommendations for engaging the community in health-care improvement through systems engineering, sharing lessons learned, and supporting research and collaborative efforts., The Baldrige Performance Excellence Program is a U.S. public-private partnership program designed to recognize and promote performance excellence in various sectors, including health care. It provides criteria for evaluating improvement efforts and shares best practices., Discussion on the integration of systems engineering in clinical education and training, highlighting initiatives by various organizations and institutions to incorporate systems-based practice and quality improvement in medical and nursing education., The document discusses policy options for education and training in health care, focusing on systems engineering to improve quality and affordability. It includes recommendations for HHS to educate clinicians, disseminate best practices, create grant programs, and fund centers of excellence., Examples of systems engineering applied to healthcare, including redesigning a hospital pharmacy, addressing alcohol abuse in San Francisco, and coordinating care in Vermont., This document provides an overview of various management and improvement methodologies such as Agile Management, Business Process Management, Complexity Science, Human Factors, Lean Enterprise System, Lean Six Sigma, Microsystem, Performance Improvement, Process Improvement, Quality Management, Queuing Theory, Flow, and the Theory of Constraints, Reliability And Maintainability, Six Sigma, Statistical Process Control, System, Systems engineering, and Systems science. It also includes an appendix of abbreviations related to healthcare and management organizations., This report describes several recommendations to support an operational national health IT infrastructure., This report discusses benefits of and challenges to enhancing health-data infrastructure. It includes recommendations for modernizing information systems, aligning data standards, and developing policies for data exchange and privacy., The document discusses the challenges and recommendations for achieving interoperability in electronic health records (EHRs) to improve healthcare and biomedical research. It highlights the need for a comprehensive software architecture, the limitations of current Meaningful Use criteria, and the importance of data integration while protecting patient privacy., Discussion on the creation of an interoperable health data infrastructure, defining software architecture, APIs for EHRs, and international interoperability for research., Continue and accelerate HHS open data activities, develop user-friendly data products and tools, accelerate release of data on health system performance, expand access to Medicare claims and other high-value data sets, invest in data methods, tools and standards, hire data scientists and engineers, demonstrate how HHS data are fueling new innovations, invite data insights and discovery, develop data partnerships, increase investments in analysis, management and dissemination of data, link and compile data from across HHS, develop business intelligence tools.

Description: An advisory report by the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology on the role of technology in the future of cities., A report by the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology on opportunities to improve urban life through technology and innovation., This report focuses on the technologies that shape key infrastructures and economic activities in urban environments, addressing challenges such as resilience against climate change and natural disasters., Discussion on the integration of technology in city infrastructure, including cleaner energy technologies, ICT, and data analytics to improve urban services and socioeconomic development., The potential of a district-based approach to improve local economies and create jobs through technological implementations in city districts, focusing on energy efficiency, mobility, and inclusivity. The role of Federal agencies and international efforts in urban innovation., Recommendations for the Federal Government to support new technologies in cities, focusing on economic opportunities, job creation, quality of life, and infrastructure improvement., Recommendations for establishing the Cities Innovation Technology Investment Initiative (CITII) to pioneer technology-enhanced cities with goals for inclusion and equity, and for HUD to embrace technological innovation to revitalize low-income communities., Recommendations for supporting cities and municipalities in developing Urban Development Districts and introducing new technology, including the creation of Qualified Public Infrastructure Bonds and an Advanced Technology Infrastructure Incubator Program. Also, the establishment of the Urban Science Technology Initiative Subcommittee to coordinate Federally funded R&D., Challenges faced by Americans living in cities are exacerbated by city growth and aging infrastructure. Advances in technology offer new approaches to addressing these challenges, but cities need support to overcome obstacles., The document discusses the impact of ICT, sensors, and autonomous vehicles on city infrastructure and services, highlighting potential cost savings and changes in land use., The development of CAVs is coming on the heels of a wave of innovation using apps, mobile devices, data, analytics, and the cloud to deliver new types of ridesharing, routing, cost avoidance, and market transparency. Intelligent transportation system (ITS) pilot programs are emerging throughout the world., The document discusses various urban sectors such as transportation, energy, building and housing, water, urban manufacturing, and urban farming, highlighting technologies and concepts aimed at improving efficiency, sustainability, and resilience. It also addresses the increasing demand for energy and the potential for transformation in energy systems., Discussion on district energy systems, renewable energy initiatives in U.S. cities, energy storage projects, and advancements in building and housing technologies., The document discusses various efforts and strategies for sustainable water management and urban planning, including storm-water capture systems and green-building initiatives., The document discusses new approaches to urban farming using soil-less systems and urban manufacturing, highlighting examples like Aerofarms in Newark and rooftop greenhouses in Chicago. It also covers the Equitable Innovation Economies Initiative aimed at fostering inclusive urban development., Understanding and adjusting tradeoffs between physical and socioeconomic transformations in cities through district-based approaches like Innovation Districts and Urban Development Districts., Discussion on green districts using design principles and technologies for sustainable development, including LEED-ND ratings, Target Cities program, and various city climate goals., U.S. cities' transportation trends post-World War II, impact of new technologies on transportation, parking space statistics in Los Angeles, Phoenix, and San Francisco, benefits of walking and biking in cities, The Seaholm district in Austin, Texas, and the Talbot Norfolk Triangle in Boston are examples of transit-oriented developments (TODs) that enhance connectivity and inclusivity through multi-modal transportation networks and smart-phone enabled services. These initiatives aim to reduce automobile usage, increase walkability, and provide affordable alternatives for older adults and low-income residents. It highlights the importance of certification and accreditation programs to create a skilled workforce for implementing new city technologies., Recommendations for a coordinated Federal effort to support technological innovation in cities, focusing on economic disparities, physical infrastructure, and creating new business opportunities and jobs., The document discusses the role of various federal agencies in promoting smart cities and technology innovation, with a focus on funding, training, and data sharing initiatives. It recommends the creation of the Urban Science Technology Initiative (USTI) Subcommittee to coordinate Federally funded R&D, focusing on urban infrastructure and services. The City Web is proposed as a platform for sharing urban solutions and data., The City Web concept aims to improve technology adoption in cities by leveraging software-as-a-service, mobile apps, and online marketplaces. It emphasizes open-source development, data sharing, and interoperability to enhance city services and infrastructure modernization. Urban Development Districts provide experimental spaces to test and implement these innovations., The City Web provides a platform for urban innovations, facilitating data accumulation and analysis to improve urban life. It involves diverse stakeholders and promotes collaboration between civic organizations, businesses, and government agencies., Exploration of city-university partnerships, public-private partnerships on infrastructure and services, democratic governance, public policy, public management, data creation, open data portals, and digital services., The number of cities opening data has grown quickly over the past 5 years, with now on the order of a hundred cities and places operating open data portals. Many cities are making much of their data publicly available in open data portals., Data generated by city governments and utilities on urban services, dynamic maps, environmental quality data, social and economic data, and the importance of data exchange and privacy-preserving analysis., APIs and other Web resources allow organizations to share data online in standard formats, enabling modular applications and mash-ups. The City Web supports developing and promoting APIs for data exchange. Open311 and GTFS are examples of successful API ecosystems in urban services and transport, respectively. APIs in the energy sector provide solar energy generation information., The document discusses the importance of data-exchange standards and APIs for urban data, particularly in the context of the Internet of Things. It highlights the need for interoperability between different urban systems and the role of predictive analytics in optimizing city operations, such as crime prediction and food safety inspections., The document discusses the integration of data models and algorithms into inspection schedules to improve public safety and efficiency. It highlights the development of tools like the Mayor's Dashboard and the City Web for data integration and analytics., The document discusses the development and use of large-scale computational models in urban applications, the integration of various data streams, and the potential of the City Web to transform urban modeling., The City Web concept involves interoperable open data formats, APIs, and modular components to support urban innovation and development. It aims to integrate various urban sectors and enhance sustainability, resiliency, accessibility, equity, transparency, security, and efficiency. The document also discusses data-enabled pilot projects focusing on public health and asthma., The document discusses various initiatives and programs in different cities aimed at combating asthma and reducing air pollution through innovative technologies and data analysis., The document discusses data-driven approaches to improve urban safety and efficiency, including Vision Zero for transportation safety, Safe Routes to School for prioritizing school safety, and FireCast for fire prevention in New York City., The document discusses the use of technology and data analytics in urban management, including crime prediction, street services, and recycling efforts in cities like Los Angeles and Chicago., The document discusses various initiatives by the Department of Commerce and other federal agencies to promote smart cities and smart growth, including the Smart America Challenge and the Global City Teams Challenge., The Economic Development Administration supports infrastructure improvements and development in distressed communities through various initiatives including the Strong Cities, Strong Communities Economic Visioning Challenge. Description: The report discusses the role of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology in providing science and technology advice to the President, with a focus on maintaining U.S. leadership in semiconductors., A report assessing the challenges and opportunities facing semiconductor innovation, competitiveness, and security, with recommendations for action., The document discusses the global semiconductor market, highlighting the influence of government and academia, national-security concerns, and industrial policies. It emphasizes the need for U.S. policy to innovate faster to mitigate risks posed by Chinese industrial policy and outlines recommendations for influencing Chinese behavior, fostering a competitive domestic industry, and driving transformative innovation., Discussion on the importance of a robust U.S. semiconductor industry for innovation, economic strength, and national security., The document discusses the changing landscape of the semiconductor industry, focusing on the shift of fabrication facilities abroad, the dominance of U.S. companies in integrated circuits, and the challenges posed by Chinese industrial policies., The semiconductor industry is facing challenges due to rising industry concentration, high costs, and Chinese industrial policies. These factors impact innovation, competition, and U.S. national security., Discussion on China's semiconductor industry strategy, including subsidies and zero-sum tactics., China employs zero-sum tactics in the semiconductor industry, including forcing domestic purchases, technology transfer, intellectual property theft, and collusion, affecting global innovation and market dynamics., Discussion on U.S. semiconductor policy and strategy to maintain leadership and innovation in the face of Chinese competition., The document discusses the potential benefits of a standing committee of industry experts for the U.S. government, strategies to promote U.S. semiconductor innovation, and responses by other countries to Chinese industrial policy in the semiconductor industry., Discussion on China's obligations under WTO Subsidies Agreement, U.S.-China semiconductor industry commitments, and U.S. recommendations for transparency and national security tools., Discussion on U.S. semiconductor strategy focusing on workforce, research, tax reform, and facility permitting to sustain innovation., Discussion on pre-competitive basic research, corporate tax reform, and facility permitting in the semiconductor industry., The document discusses strategies for maintaining U.S. leadership in the semiconductor industry, including reviewing federal permitting, creating fast track options, increasing staff capacity, and developing a leapfrog strategy for innovation., Recommendations for U.S. policymakers to select ambitious challenges, called 'moonshots', to drive computing and semiconductor innovation forward. These moonshots aim to catalyze activity, accelerate innovation, and create new technologies with society-wide benefits., Discussion on semiconductor technology moonshots, industry investment, and government role in R&D and commercialization., Coordination of moonshots across the U.S. government to drive advances in systems and component technologies, with a focus on common commercial and government interests. Establishment of advisory groups across industry, government, and academia to support moonshots., Examples of moonshots in semiconductor innovation including zero day bio-threat detection network, high efficiency global weather forecasting system, and commercial quantum computers for computational chemistry and materials science., Post-quantum cryptography, Non-Von Neumann computing elements, quantum computers, moonshot challenges, semiconductor innovations, incentive prizes, U.S. Government Fellowship, Collaborative Institute, Industry-Led Venture Capital Consortium, The report discusses the challenges faced by the semiconductor industry and the importance of coordinated efforts among government, industry, and academia. It introduces the concept of moonshots to drive innovation across the technology stack., Discussion on various computing modalities and architectural approaches including Von Neumann, Quantum, Bio/neuro-inspired, Analog computing, Special purpose architectures, and Approximate Computing. It covers the potential advancements and challenges in these areas., Analysis of various component technologies, their time-frame to first commercial products, and approaches to achieving and retaining competitive advantage. Description: An advisory report by the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology focusing on independence, technology, and connection in older age., The report focuses on technology's role in increasing the quality of life for older adults, addressing social engagement, cognitive function, and physical ability, with recommendations for Federal actions., The report identifies technologies and policies to maximize the independence, productivity, and engagement of older Americans, focusing on social connectivity, cognitive change, and physical change., The document discusses the impact of technology on older adults, focusing on social participation, cognitive changes, and physical ability. It highlights the importance of internet access, emergency communication systems, monitoring technologies, and protection against financial fraud., Recommendations for integrating federal action, engagement and social connectivity, and monitoring technology for frail and vulnerable elders to support independent aging., A series of recommendations aimed at improving technology and services for older adults, focusing on areas such as privacy, security, education, emergency response, financial services, cognitive training, telehealth, home design, product design, and assistive technologies., The United States is an aging society with increasing life expectancy and healthier aging trends. Challenges include chronic diseases and functional limitations. Caregivers and supportive services are critical for older adults, many of whom wish to age in place., Potential future health challenges for older adults and the role of technology in supporting them, The study identified technologies that address multiple goals for older adults, including supporting independence, socialization, engagement, education, self-management of chronic diseases, quality of life, access to health care, safety, security, and cost management. It also examined barriers to technology adoption and recommended strategies for development and adoption., Technological advances can help older Americans continue working, participate in the sharing economy, and work remotely. However, older workers face challenges in finding jobs that fit their capabilities. Caregivers play a critical role in assisting seniors and need technology to help them meet their responsibilities. The report highlights the heterogeneity of the older-adult population and the need for versatile technologies., The document discusses the application of user-centered design and universal design for older adults, the role of Internet connectivity in reducing social isolation and providing telehealth services, the challenges faced by older adults in accessing the Internet, the role of Federal agencies in providing services for aging adults, and the growing role of monitoring technologies in homes and communities., The document discusses the use of technology to enhance the aging experience, focusing on interdisciplinary research, standards, and recommendations for federal action, social connectivity, monitoring technology, and innovation., The document discusses the role of technology in promoting social connectivity and emotional health among older adults, highlighting the importance of social participation and the impact of technology on engagement and health outcomes., The document discusses the use of technology to support older adults, including applications like Vincles and Honor, and the impact of employment and volunteerism on older adults' quality of life., Discussion on how new technologies can help older adults leverage their skills for work or volunteering, access information, and maintain independence., The document discusses the utilization and adoption of technology among older adults, highlighting disparities in access to the Internet and broadband based on income, education, and race., Improving affordability, accessibility, training, and usability of technology for older people is critical for increasing usage. The Federal Government can take several steps to improve these factors., Internet use among older adults, broadband access in rural areas, technology training for older adults, employment and technology skills gap, OATS partners with various organizations to establish broadband adoption ecosystems for older adults, providing access, training, and support tailored to seniors' needs. It operates Senior Planet Exploration Centers and mobile labs, offering free training and online learning modules. HUD's Service Coordinator Program and CNCS's Senior Corps are also involved in improving technology access and training for older adults., The document discusses the challenges faced by older adults during technological transitions and emergencies, with a focus on Superstorm Sandy. It highlights the reliance on landlines, lack of redundant communication, and efforts by organizations like The Red Hook Initiative to provide connectivity., Older people are especially vulnerable in disaster and emergency situations. Redundant power sources are critical for those dependent on medical equipment. FEMA and other agencies should improve emergency management and communication systems for older people., The document discusses the role of federal agencies in advancing communication systems for older adults, promoting interoperability of medical information, and supporting cognitive health technologies., The document discusses technologies that help older adults manage cognitive impairments, including in-home sensing, wearable technologies, and mobile applications. It highlights the potential of these technologies to maintain cognitive health and independence., Smart technologies show promise in detecting changes in cognition and functional performance that may be indicative of cognitive decline and impairment. Before the large-scale deployment of these systems can occur, however, several issues need to be addressed. There is limited evidence, especially from large-scale studies, on the feasibility, validity, reliability, and comparative effectiveness of these approaches. There is more to learn about implementation, such as the optimal monitoring schedule, usability, and cost. While many older adults are comfortable with the privacy implications of monitoring, more work is needed on privacy and security. Cognitive impairment can often reduce a person's ability to manage finances ('financial capacity'). When Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, or similar diseases become symptomatic, declines in financial capacity are typically even greater. Compared to younger adults, older adults may be more likely to make poor financial decisions that depend on recent learning, although older adults are likely to exhibit less risk taking if a decision relies on well-learned behaviors. Changes in financial capacity—skills, knowledge, or judgment—are among the reasons that older adults are more likely to be victims of financial fraud and exploitation., The document discusses financial capacity in patients with cognitive impairments, elder financial abuse, and the role of financial institutions in preventing fraud and exploitation., Studies and reports on financial exploitation of seniors, impact of financial capacity loss due to Alzheimer's, and initiatives to combat elder financial abuse., The document discusses the need for a national strategy to combat elder financial exploitation, highlighting the role of Adult Protective Service agencies, the Bank Secrecy Act, and technological solutions like algorithms and monitoring systems., The document discusses the challenges and barriers to adopting technologies for monitoring elder abuse in financial transactions, including privacy concerns and the lack of industry-wide adoption of algorithms., The Federal Government should encourage the banking and financial services sector to offer monitoring services to protect assets from fraud and exploitation. The document discusses the importance of identifying declines in financial capacity among older adults and protecting them from fraud or exploitation., Studies on cognitive training effects on older adults, retention of trained skills, and transferability to other tasks. Concerns about the commercial brain training industry and the need for regulatory review by the FTC., Effects of cognitive training interventions with older adults, task coordination and aging, ten-year effects of cognitive training, impact of cognitive training and mental stimulation, long-term effects of cognitive training, cognitive assistive technologies, cognitive coaching and prompting systems, assurance systems, compensation systems, COACH prompting system, socialization enhancement through technology., Mobility and successful aging are inextricably intertwined. Sustained mobility is a key ingredient for independence, quality of life, community participation, and-as needed or desired-employment for older adults. Successful aging in place heavily depends on an individual's ability to remain mobile in and around his or her home, to maintain normal daily activities, and to access appropriate nutrition. Mobility loss is frequently a precursor to declining health and increased costs of care. Falls are a common problem. Over one-third of older adults reported a fall within a recent two year period. Injuries due to falls are a frequent cause for emergency room visits by older adults, and unintentional falls are the leading cause of death by injury for adults over 65 years old. There are multiple technologies that could improve mobility. Power wheelchairs, manual wheelchairs, walkers, and scooters are in common use now, and there are growing capabilities in prosthetic devices and robotic assistants. Several United States-based programs, such as those offered by the Department of Veterans Affairs, show potential approaches to meeting a spectrum of mobility needs. There are multiple barriers to mobility for older adults. Architectural barriers in homes, buildings, and the environment may limit an individual's mobility, and it may further limit mobility aids like scooters or walkers. Commercially available technologies such as hands-free faucets and door openers are rarely available in private homes. Post-construction architectural modifications to increase the accessibility of a home often are difficult or have high cost. Inaccessible or hard-to-use fixtures, cabinets, and furniture can make normal daily activities a challenge; difficulty reaching items or difficulty transferring on and off the toilet or in and out of a tub, chair, or bed create significant barriers to daily living. Kitchen appliances with challenging interfaces or food sealed in difficult-to-open packaging may make accessing proper nutrition a problem. There are multiple ways to define mobility, which has implications for judging the success of a particular technology or treatment. There are clinical assessments that measure a person's ability to walk a series of steps, to rise from a chair, or to exhibit fine-motor skills. Beyond that, others look at independence, such as whether an individual is mobile enough to conduct basic activities of daily living or take part in the community. A recurring theme is the tension between providing targeted medical treatment, in some cases very expensive medical treatment, without sufficient consideration for comprehensive, Discussion on telehealth technologies and their impact on healthcare access, particularly for older adults and rural communities. Includes the role of telehealth in expanding access to specialty care and enhancing local healthcare workforce expertise., Project ECHO is a technology-mediated consultation model that extends healthcare expertise to rural areas, initially for Hepatitis C and now for various chronic illnesses. It includes training for community health workers and is applied in correctional care. Telehealth technologies are used for remote patient monitoring and cancer services in rural areas., Several Federal agencies use telehealth technologies to directly provide health care. The Veterans Health Administration provides patient care using telehealth, including mental health and ICU monitoring. The Department of Defense uses telehealth for direct patient care, and TRICARE reimburses for telehealth services. The Indian Health Service provides telehealth services to Native American, Alaska Native, and Pacific-Islander populations. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services support telehealth in Medicare and Medicaid programs. The Department of Defense operates research centers for telemedicine technologies., The document discusses telehealth adoption in US hospitals, factors influencing it, and various federal initiatives and programs supporting telehealth and aging in place., The evidence behind telehealth reflects its evolution and challenges in implementation, highlighting both benefits and limitations. Studies show telehealth can reduce mortality risks and healthcare costs for chronic diseases, but some forms have not improved care. Policy barriers like professional licensure and reimbursement limit telehealth's potential., The document discusses the role of telehealth in improving access to healthcare, especially in underserved areas, and the importance of home design in maintaining independence for older adults., The document discusses the importance of home modifications and assistive technologies in preventing functional decline and promoting independence among older adults. It highlights the need for streamlined regulations and payment policies to support home accessibility standards, especially in retirement communities. The role of product design in compensating for mobility losses due to arthritis is also emphasized., The document discusses the challenges faced by older adults with packaging, the impact on nutrition and safety, and recommendations for improving product design to meet their needs., Advances in wheelchairs and other mobility technologies, policy challenges in accessibility, and recommendations for future improvements.

Description: The President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) is an advisory group of the Nation's leading scientists and engineers, appointed by the President to augment the science and technology advice available to him from inside the White House and from cabinet departments and other Federal agencies., A report by the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) on ensuring the safety of the nation's drinking water, highlighting recommendations for federal agencies and partners to improve water safety through science and technology., The report discusses the challenges and recommendations for ensuring safe drinking water in the United States, highlighting issues such as contamination, aging infrastructure, and the role of science and technology., The document discusses the systems and challenges related to drinking-water contamination in the United States, including the susceptibility of ground and surface water to various contaminants and the impact of climate change on water quality and quantity., The document discusses climate-related impacts on water quality and quantity, contamination issues at drinking-water treatment plants, and distribution systems. It highlights the challenges posed by various contaminants, including inorganic and organic chemicals, radionuclides, and microbes, as well as the effects of corrosion in distribution systems and premise plumbing., Discussion on the regulatory framework for drinking-water safety in the United States, focusing on the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) and its amendments, the role of the EPA, and the establishment of primary and secondary drinking-water standards., Discussion on lead contamination in drinking water, historical sources of lead exposure, and regulatory measures by EPA and FDA., Discussion on drinking-water contaminants, health impacts, monitoring issues, and EPA regulations., Discussion on EPA rules for monitoring water contaminants, challenges in water treatment plants, and issues related to lead pipes in U.S. communities., The document discusses historical and current practices in water treatment, including the use of chemical disinfectants, biological filtration, and emerging technologies such as micro- or ultrafiltration membranes and ultraviolet-based disinfection. It highlights the need for innovation in areas like nitrate and arsenic removal, reverse osmosis efficiency, and monitoring technologies., New sensors are continually becoming available, allowing for new streams of data to be collected by water systems. These sensors can measure multiple parameters and help assess the integrity of the distribution system. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) deployed the first-ever freshwater environmental sample processor (ESP) for algal toxins. Leak detection plays a major role in maintaining distribution-system integrity. Continuous acoustic monitoring (CAM) equipment can detect leaks early. The Environmental Protection Agency conducts research on microbial and chemical contaminants and maintains the Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS)., The document discusses various federal agencies and their roles in monitoring and improving drinking water quality, including USGS's monitoring and modeling activities, NOAA's work on Harmful Algal Bloom prediction, CDC's focus on preventing diseases from water contamination, NSF's support for scientific research related to water treatment, and interagency consortia efforts., The EPA Drinking-Water Action Plan aims to address challenges in the drinking-water system through engagement across the Federal Government, water utilities, and stakeholders. It focuses on six priorities including equity in water-infrastructure, oversight approaches, source-water protection, addressing unregulated contaminants, improving transparency, and reducing lead risks., The document discusses the expansion of drinking-water-monitoring technologies, recommendations for water testing for vulnerable populations, and the need for big-data analytics in drinking-water systems., Recommendations for developing a Drinking Water Data Platform, increasing data collection through citizen science, and developing the drinking-water treatment and distribution-system workforce., Supports water-quality education programs at community colleges, development of a blueprint for professional development of water treatment operators, federal coordination of research and development focused on safe drinking water., The document discusses the creation of a new research entity to develop technologies for improving drinking water safety, including cataloging current programs, surveying non-Federal actors, identifying unmet needs, and securing funding. It also recommends developing transformational technologies and outlines early research topics., Recommendations for improving methodologies and developing data for comparative-risk assessments of drinking-water contaminants, and deploying city-based safe drinking-water demonstration projects., The report addresses the challenges of maintaining high-quality drinking water in the United States, focusing on science and technology's role in ensuring safety, particularly in light of crises like Flint, Michigan. It includes recommendations for Federal agencies and partners to develop advancements for a safe and reliable drinking water supply., Overview of drinking-water systems and contamination issues, regulatory oversight, and recommendations for safe drinking water., Ground water and surface water are susceptible to contamination by sewage, industrial, mining, and agricultural wastes, and other pollutants. Over half of surface water intakes for facilities serving more than 10,000 people are impacted by upstream wastewater discharge., The document discusses the impacts of climate change on water systems, including increased water temperatures, decreased snowpack, sea level rise, droughts, and heavy precipitation events. It highlights the challenges faced by water utilities and the need for adaptation and resilience activities., Discussion on water-treatment technologies, contamination issues in distribution systems, and the impact of corrosion on water quality., The document discusses the challenges and risks associated with premise plumbing and distribution systems, including microbial and chemical contamination, the use of plastics, and the impact of transmission main degradation., The document discusses the costs and techniques associated with the renovation and replacement of drinking water distribution pipes, highlighting alternative methods to traditional open-trench techniques., The Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) establishes the framework for regulating public water supplies to ensure safe drinking water. It includes primary and secondary standards, testing, and treatment requirements., Summary of key federal regulations including the Safe Drinking Water Act, Clean Water Act, Lead and Copper Rule, and Microbial and Disinfection ByProduct Rule cluster., Recommendations and revisions related to the Lead and Copper Rule, focusing on minimizing exposure to lead in drinking water and integrating cross-media lead reduction efforts., Discussion on risk assessment, population risk, societal risk, and comparative-risk methodologies related to environmental hazards and public health., Discussion on the complexities of drinking-water contaminants, focusing on chlorination and disinfection byproducts, and the challenges of balancing risks in water treatment., Discussion on the role of chlorine and chloramine in corrosion, elevated blood lead levels due to contaminated water, and monitoring issues related to drinking water safety., Discussion on the challenges and violations in U.S. drinking-water systems, including specific cases like Flint, Michigan, and the criteria for mandatory reporting and remediation of contaminants., Lead pipes are a national issue, especially in older cities and the Midwest. The Flint, Michigan water crisis highlights the dangers of lead contamination and the need for proper water treatment and monitoring., The report discusses the Flint water crisis, government failures, lead contamination, and public health responses., The document discusses the replacement of lead service lines in Flint and the impact of harmful algal blooms in Toledo, Ohio, including the response and remedial actions taken., The document discusses historical and recent trends in water treatment practices, focusing on disinfection methods and innovations in technology such as UV light and biological filtration., Discussion on nitrate and arsenic removal from water, challenges with current technologies, and innovations needed. Overview of monitoring technologies for water quality, including sensors and their deployment., Research on safe drinking water, leak detection, and water quality monitoring., The document outlines the efforts of various U.S. federal agencies in monitoring, modeling, and ensuring safe drinking water, including research on water quality, harmful algal bloom prediction, disease prevention, and interagency collaborations., The EPA Drinking Water Action Plan aims to address challenges in the drinking-water system through engagement across the Federal Government, water utilities, and stakeholders, focusing on six priorities including equity, oversight, source-water protection, unregulated contaminants, transparency, and lead risk reduction., Recommendations to improve the safety of the Nation's drinking-water system, focusing on monitoring contaminants, data sharing, citizen-science projects, and workforce training., The document discusses the inefficiencies of the current EPA sampling approach for lead abatement and suggests targeting high-risk groups such as pregnant women, infants, and young children for water testing and treatment. It highlights the role of WIC in referring participants to water testing programs., Proposal for a water testing program targeting pregnant women enrolled in WIC, focusing on lead and other contaminants in drinking water, with potential funding and coordination from EPA, HUD, and USDA., Recommendations for increased monitoring of drinking-water contaminants, especially for vulnerable populations, and the use of big data analytics to improve coordination in drinking-water systems., Development of data storage and delivery tools and standards for hydrologic data, improvement of drinking-water quality data collection and sharing, proposal for a national e-reporting rule for SDWA compliance data, collaboration between EPA and USGS for Water Quality Portal, Discussion on citizen science initiatives for monitoring drinking-water contaminants and the role of public participation in scientific data collection., The document discusses the role of citizen science in safe drinking water, emphasizing the importance of participant training and data collection precision. It also lists various water-related citizen-science activities and projects., The report identifies citizen science as a critical opportunity for EPA to strengthen public support for its mission and discusses mechanisms by which EPA can embrace, invest, and enable the use of citizen science data., The response to water contamination in Flint, Michigan, led to citizen-science efforts and highlighted the need for workforce development in water infrastructure., The NSF's ATE program supports the development of innovative approaches for educating skilled technicians for the water industry, emphasizing partnerships with community colleges and industry to improve technical skills and STEM preparation., The document discusses the need for increased investment in workforce development for drinking-water systems, including near-term and long-term opportunities for funding and training. It highlights the importance of operator certification and the need to update guidelines to incorporate advances in technology and knowledge., Recommendations for a Federal strategy to coordinate research and development for safe drinking water, including the development of innovative technologies and city-based demonstration pilots., The document discusses the creation of a new entity to develop a Federal Strategy for drinking water safety, including cataloging current programs, surveying non-Federal actors, identifying unmet needs, and securing funding. It emphasizes the need for new technologies to improve drinking water safety and encourages interagency collaboration and learning from successful programs like DARPA and ARPA-E., Current technologies offer solutions to many of the challenges facing the drinking-water-system infrastructure. There is a critical need for the development and deployment of additional innovative technologies to improve the safety of drinking water. Examples of potential water-research projects include open innovation and grand challenge coordination, and microbiome of water systems from source to tap., The document discusses the need for improved technologies and methods in water management, including sampling campaigns, brine disposal technologies, distribution system rehabilitation, water purification for oxidized pollutants, ex-situ sensing of groundwater quality, and low-cost water quality sensors., The document discusses the need for new technologies to improve the safety of drinking water, including reducing chlorine-based disinfectants and improving public-health outcome assessments., Comparative assessment of contaminants in public water systems against EPA's Maximum Contaminant Levels using data from the second 6-year review dataset under the SDWA (6YR2, 1999-2005)., Data from USEPA Six Year Review 2 (6YR2) national occurrence of 69 regulated contaminants (1999-2005). Bars represent national percentile values of individual Public Water System 90th percentile concentrations as a ratio of the corresponding contaminant Maximum Contaminant Level. The analysis could be refined using Disability/Quality Adjusted Life-Years methodologies. Advances in risk assessment methodologies and detection technologies are discussed., The document discusses the development of comparative risk assessment methodologies for drinking water utilities, focusing on system vulnerability assessments and innovative approaches in American cities., El Paso, Texas is located on the United States/Mexico border along the Rio Grande River. The population of the city of El Paso is approaching 700,000 people and the population in the region exceeds 1.1 million. Fort Bliss is a U.S. Army base just east of El Paso. The El Paso region has four distinct water sources that offer a range of advanced treatment technologies. Fresno, California is the largest city in California's Central Valley, facing economic challenges and shifting from groundwater to surface water reliance., Fresno's water sources include groundwater and surface water, with plans to reduce groundwater reliance. Cincinnati's water sources include the Ohio River and groundwater wells, with challenges related to aging infrastructure and lead service lines., The Environmental Protection Agency, in conjunction with other federal departments, should consider deploying city-based safe drinking-water demonstration projects to test and implement new technologies for water safety and quality., A list of acronyms and their meanings related to water regulations, environmental policies, and various organizations.

Description: A letter from PCAST to the President discussing the impact of technology on the workforce and the need for coordinated efforts to address job-skill mismatches., The middle-skill segment focuses on IT jobs requiring both literacy and technology skills. DARPA's Digital Tutor program simulates expert tutoring for IT training, showing significant success in a pilot study with Navy students., The difficulty employers face in filling middle-skill jobs due to skill signaling and the need for alternative credentials. The importance of the worker-trainer-employer triangle in adapting to labor-market changes., The document discusses the evolving landscape of middle-skill training options, emphasizing a new bimodal paradigm of the 'student-employee' and the role of IT in enhancing training and job matching., Tools for current and future workers, employers, and education and training organizations to improve career choices, job-search processes, skills assessments, and job-forecasting., The document discusses the importance of standardized job and skill descriptions, the role of web-based businesses in aggregating and analyzing job data, and the need for education and training programs to align with employer needs. It highlights initiatives like the Job-Driven Community College Grants and the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act to improve data collection and reporting on employment outcomes., Discussion on the role of career and technical education (CTE) in preparing for middle-skill jobs, the impact of technology on CTE, and the significance of programs like TAACCCT and MOOCs., Evaluation and leveraging of lessons learned from the Advanced Technological Education (ATE) at the National Science Foundation (NSF) and other organizations are essential. Reports indicate that many of the students who were most likely to complete the initial MOOCs were highly self-motivated individuals. Udacity offers career-counseling services, while edX ventured into the jobs-matching space. The Federal Government can promote validation of skills assessments and associated credentials through competency-based assessments., Discussion on MOOCs, competency-based assessments, and integration of education and labor market systems., Recommendations for improving the worker-trainer-employer ecosystem, supporting IT development for skills assessment and training, and Federal Government's role in using IT for workforce development.
